reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Distinguished by paradoxical myotonia, in which stiffness worsens rather than improves with repeated activity, the opposite of the warm-up seen in myotonia congenita
Symptoms are markedly precipitated or aggravated by cold exposure, classically affecting the face, eyelids, tongue and hands
Cold-induced stiffness can be followed by a period of flaccid weakness that may persist for some time after rewarming
Caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SCN4A skeletal-muscle sodium channel gene and inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern
It sits on a clinical continuum with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis and the potassium-aggravated myotonias, all allelic SCN4A disorders
Management combines avoidance of cold and other triggers with sodium-channel-blocking antimyotonic agents when symptoms are troublesome
Bedside cooling of a hand, or asking the patient to repeatedly forcefully close the eyes, can reproduce the paradoxical worsening
reference.pathophysiology: Paramyotonia congenita is caused by gain-of-function mutations in SCN4A, encoding the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.4. The mutant channels show impaired or slowed inactivation, and this defect is temperature sensitive so that cooling exaggerates the persistent sodium current. Incomplete inactivation produces sustained membrane depolarisation, which at moderate levels causes repetitive firing perceived as myotonia and, when depolarisation becomes severe, inactivates the remaining channels to render the fibre inexcitable and weak. Because the abnormality worsens with sustained activity and with cold, patients experience the characteristic paradoxical, cold-sensitive myotonia followed by weakness rather than the warm-up improvement of chloride channelopathies.
additionalInvestigations: Electromyography with myotonic discharges, including recordings before and after muscle cooling
Short exercise electromyography protocol with cooling, showing the characteristic decrement pattern
Serum creatine kinase and interictal potassium
Assessment to exclude myotonic dystrophy and its systemic features
Muscle biopsy only where diagnostic uncertainty persists
redFlags: Prolonged or severe cold-induced weakness impairing safe function
Respiratory or bulbar involvement during a severe episode
Susceptibility to anaesthetic complications with depolarising muscle relaxants and hypothermia
Emergence of a fixed myopathy, which would prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Paramyotonia congenita is a non-progressive disorder compatible with a normal lifespan, and although cold-triggered stiffness and weakness can be disabling in cold climates or occupations, symptoms are usually manageable with trigger avoidance and antimyotonic therapy.
pitfalls: Confusing the paradoxical cold-worsened myotonia with the warm-up improvement of myotonia congenita
Failing to test after cooling, so mild or intermittent myotonia is missed on standard examination or electromyography
Not recognising the overlap with hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis when weakness dominates
Overlooking anaesthetic risks from cold theatres and depolarising neuromuscular blockade
